paragraphs.text: The paperless office was announced in 1975, in a magazine article that gave it about fifteen years. The prediction was reasonable: screens were getting cheaper, storage was getting smaller, and everything a filing cabinet did could be done better by a computer. What happened instead is one of the better-documented failures of forecasting. Office paper consumption rose through the 1980s and 1990s, roughly tracking the spread of the personal computer and, above all, the cheap laser printer. Each new machine that was supposed to replace paper turned out to be an excellent device for producing more of it. The story is worth telling not because the forecast was wrong, but because of what the error revealed about what paper was actually for.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Researchers who watched people work found out why. Paper is not a storage medium that screens happen to beat; it is a tool with properties that were invisible until someone tried to remove it. Sheets can be spread across a desk so that four documents are visible at once, which no single screen of the period could match. They can be annotated anywhere, in any direction, without a menu. They can be handed to someone, and the handing is itself a message. Above all they are easy to arrange in space: piles on a desk are not mess but a memory system, and their owner can usually say what is in each one.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The turning point, when it came, was not a better screen but a better set of conventions. Paper use in offices peaked around the middle of the 2000s and has fallen since, in most measures by a third or more. What changed was that documents stopped being things and started being processes: signatures became clicks, forms became fields, and approval stopped being a sheet that travelled between desks. Once a document had no paper original anywhere in its life, printing it became an odd thing to do rather than the default one.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Reading, though, has been slower to move than filing. Studies comparing the same text on paper and on screen find small but stubborn differences: on screen, readers are worse at remembering where something was in a document, they skim more and re-read less, and they judge their own understanding more generously than their test scores justify. The gap is largest for long, difficult texts and nearly disappears for short ones. It also narrows with practice and with better software, which suggests that some of it is habit rather than physiology — but it has not vanished in thirty years of trying.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The environmental arithmetic is less obvious than the campaigns suggest. Paper is heavy, and making it uses water and energy, but the fibre is renewable and most of it is now recycled at least once. A screen is made from materials that are mined, is powered continuously, and is replaced every few years. The honest comparison depends on how long the document is read and on how the electricity is made: a page printed once and thrown away is worse than reading it on a device you already own, while a laptop bought to avoid printing a single report is worse than the report.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Where paper survives, it survives for reasons that have little to do with nostalgia. Hospitals keep paper drug charts as a fallback that works when the network does not. Pilots and engineers keep paper checklists because a sheet cannot run out of battery in the middle of a procedure. Courts keep signed originals because a physical document is harder to alter without leaving a trace. In each case the paper is not the main system; it is the part of the system that has to keep working when the main one stops.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The lesson is duller than either side of the argument wanted. Paper was never defeated by screens, and it was never going to defeat them; it was displaced from the tasks screens do better, kept for the tasks it does better, and quietly redesigned around the tasks that are now shared between the two. The office of 2030 will still have paper in it, just as the office of 1995 already had computers. The question worth asking of any workflow is not whether it is paperless but whether each piece of paper in it is doing something a screen genuinely cannot.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: About a quarter of the carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels has ended up in the sea. Some of it simply dissolves, as it would in any cold liquid, but a substantial part is moved downwards by life. Microscopic plants in the sunlit surface take carbon out of the water as they grow; a fraction of that carbon eventually sinks below the depth at which the water mixes with the surface again, and once it is down there it is out of the atmosphere for centuries. Oceanographers call the whole arrangement the biological pump, and it is the reason the sea holds more carbon than it otherwise would.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The sinking material is unglamorous. Dead cells clump together with mucus and mineral grains into flakes that drift down at a few tens of metres a day, and a diver in clear water can watch them fall like weather. The rest of the descent is faster and less pleasant: zooplankton eat the flakes at the surface and release dense pellets that fall in hours rather than weeks, and animals that feed at night near the surface and rest by day at depth carry carbon down in their bodies and leave it there. Roughly ninety per cent of what starts to sink is eaten or dissolved on the way and never reaches the deep.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: That last figure is why small changes matter so much. If the proportion reaching a kilometre down shifts by a few percentage points, the amount of carbon stored for centuries changes by an amount comparable to the emissions of a large country. Depth is what turns a temporary store into a long one: material stopped at two hundred metres returns to the surface within a year or two, while material that passes a kilometre is unlikely to come back before the water itself circulates, which in the Pacific takes something like a thousand years.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Measuring any of this is hard. The traditional instrument is a sediment trap, a funnel moored for months at a chosen depth, which catches what falls into it and preserves the sample in brine. Traps are reliable and produce one number per mooring, which is not enough to map an ocean. Newer methods watch the water instead: floats that drift for years and dive daily, and gliders that fly slow transects, carry optical sensors which count the flakes as flashes of scattered light. The difficulty is that a float sees a column of water a few centimetres across, and the ocean it is asked to describe is patchy at every scale.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The pump also runs differently in different places, which is why global averages mislead. In the North Atlantic a spring bloom produces a short, heavy fall of material; in the subtropical gyres, where the surface is warm and nutrients are scarce, the pump is weak all year; near the equator and along coasts with upwelling it is strong and steady. Warming affects these regions unequally: a warmer surface layer mixes less with the water beneath it, which starves the plants of nutrients in some regions and, in others, keeps them in the light for longer.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: This has made the pump attractive to people looking for ways to remove carbon deliberately. Proposals include adding iron to regions where its absence limits growth, pumping nutrient-rich water upwards, and sinking crop residues. All of them are limited by the same arithmetic: most of what grows is recycled near the surface, so the fraction actually stored is small, and verifying that anything was stored at all requires measurements the field does not yet have at scale. Several experiments produced a bloom and no measurable storage, which is a useful result and an unwelcome one.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: What can be said with confidence is modest. The pump moves several billion tonnes of carbon below the mixed layer every year; it is one of the reasons the atmosphere is not warmer than it is; and current models disagree with each other about how it will respond to a warmer ocean by amounts large enough to matter for policy. The measurements now being made by floats will settle some of that disagreement within a decade. Until then, the safest assumption is that the pump is doing a service that would be expensive to replace and that nobody has yet shown how to enlarge on purpose.
paragraphs.label: G

texts.title: How loud should a city be?

paragraphs.text: Noise is the pollutant people complain about most and regulators treat least seriously. It leaves no residue, it cannot be photographed, and the damage it does is statistical rather than visible: a road that raises night-time levels across a district produces no identifiable victim, only a slightly worse distribution of sleep and blood pressure across thousands of people. Health agencies now put the burden of European traffic noise in the same order of magnitude as several well-known environmental risks, which is a strong claim built on evidence that is genuinely contested. The four researchers below agree that noise does harm and disagree about almost everything after that: how large the harm is, how to measure it, and who is supposed to pay for the quiet.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Ingrid Holm works on what noise does to sleep. Her recordings show that a sleeper reacts to a passing lorry without waking: heart rate rises, the stage of sleep shifts, and the person reports in the morning that they slept through. Over years, she argues, those unnoticed reactions are what connect night noise to blood pressure and to cardiovascular disease, and because the sleeper does not remember them, surveys that ask people whether noise bothers them miss most of the exposure. Any limit set from annoyance surveys, on this view, is set far too high. She adds that the effect is strongest where night noise is uneven, which is why a single road can matter more than a busier one that never falls silent.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Paul Achebe accepts the physiology and objects to the arithmetic. The studies that produce the headline numbers are observational: they compare people living on loud streets with people living on quiet ones, and those groups differ in income, in housing quality, in air pollution and in almost everything else that affects a heart. Statistical adjustment can reduce that problem but not remove it, and the few studies that changed the noise rather than the neighbourhood — around an airport that closed, for example — show real effects that are smaller than the observational estimates. He is not arguing that noise is harmless; he is arguing that the published figures are too confident. His preferred remedy is duller than a headline: keep the limits, publish the uncertainty with them, and fund the studies that change the noise rather than the sample.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Mei Tanaka thinks both are measuring the wrong quantity. Regulations work in average decibels over a night or a year, because averages are what monitors produce cheaply, but an average hides the structure of the sound. Ten lorries an hour at a steady level disturb less than two motorcycles at unpredictable moments, and a constant hum is easier to sleep through than a pattern that keeps the brain waiting for the next event. Her group builds measures based on the number and sharpness of events rather than the mean, and finds that they predict complaints and sleep disruption better than the official index does. Regulators have been slow to adopt such measures, she notes, because an index that cannot be produced by an existing monitor is an index that requires new equipment on every street.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Samir Oyelowo looks at who is exposed. In every city his group has mapped, the loudest housing is the cheapest, along the main roads and under the flight paths, and the people in it are least able to move or to install triple glazing. Quiet, he argues, has quietly become a purchased good: the same city can be restful or exhausting depending on which side of it you can afford. He is sceptical of solutions that depend on individual insulation for exactly this reason, and prefers measures that reduce the source — lower speed limits, quieter surfaces, electric buses, night delivery bans — because they benefit everyone on the street at once.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The policy question is what to do while the evidence is argued over. Source measures are cheap and popular: resurfacing a road can take several decibels off, which is more than most double glazing achieves, and a speed limit of thirty kilometres an hour is quieter as well as safer. Insulation helps the individual and does nothing for the street, and it fails in summer when windows are open. The awkward truth is that the most effective measure is also the least popular, because it means fewer and slower vehicles in places where people are used to driving.
paragraphs.label: F
